children: 1446 ET - The surge in U.S. consumer confidence observed in the latest Conference Board survey was supported by a resilient labor market and lower gasoline prices, LPL Financial's Jeffrey Roach says in a note. Consumers are moving past election-related uncertainty and finding some relief at the pump, which has an outsized impact on perceptions of the economy even if gasoline only accounts for a relatively small share of household spending, Roach says. Homebuying plans also rebounded in November despite the increase in mortgage rates, he says. Consumer spending should continue to power economic growth this quarter, Roach says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1357 ET - Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem went to great lengths to suggest his thinking about inflation risks haven't changed amid a drop in energy prices and weak employment data, says Avery Shenfeld, chief economist at CIBC World Markets. Macklem's speech in Toronto "seemed to downplay some of the disinflationary momentum seen of late," says Shenfeld in a note to clients, in which he preps them for another BOC hike in December. In a question-and-answer session following the speech, Shenfeld says Macklem emphasized how October's quarter-point rate increase was "starting from the lower end of the neutral range." After a December hike, Shenfeld says ample evidence should arrive before the scheduled January decision to persuade the BOC to keep its policy rate unchanged. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1352 ET - Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem's speech likely sets the stage for a second straight rate hike in December, says Royce Mendes, head of macro strategy at Desjardins Group. Macklem's remarks gave more weight to worries over anticipated upward--and persistent--pressure on prices, versus relief from a recent drop in energy costs, Mendes says. He adds Macklem referred to economic activity as rather resilient, despite some weak readings on employment. Mendes says another quarter-point increase in the BOC policy rate, to 2.75%, "will limit the spread of energy-related price increases," and reinforce the BOC's commitment to achieve and maintain 2% total inflation. "The speech as delivered was clearly hawkish," Mendes says. (paul.vieira@wsj.com, @paulvieira)

1323 ET - Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem makes clear in a speech in Toronto that the BOC targets 2% total inflation. Macklem adds BOC officials will lean on two gauges of core--CPI-trim and CPIX--to understand underlying trends, and for use in its overall forecast. But headline inflation will be the guiding light. "Our main core measures can miss parts of the inflation story," Macklem says. "No single measure can give us the whole picture." Macklem adds that households found BOC repeated references to core "confusing" because items like food and gas--which are excluded from core--are everyday items. Further, Macklem says some financial-market participants "sometimes felt that we were moving the inflation goalposts" with frequent talk of core CPI.  (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1300 ET - According to annual revisions released by the Federal Reserve, U.S. industrial capacity is estimated to have expanded at a slower pace in recent years than previously estimated. Capacity growth averaged 1% per year after 2022, revised down from 1.2%. Annual industrial capacity growth from 2023 through 2025 was revised down by an average of 0.4 percentage point, while growth in 2026 was revised up by 0.3 percentage point. Meanwhile, capacity utilization was revised up by an average of 0.8 percentage point from 2023 through 2025. Overall industrial production in October 2026 was 3.6% above its level at the end of 2022, unchanged from the previous estimate, the report says.(jessica.coacci@wsj.com)

1230 ET - Bitcoin was the canary in the coal mine for recent market losses, analysts at Glassnode say in a research note. It was the first asset to give back recent rally gains, with stocks being slower to react but eventually coming under pressure, they say. The flagship cryptocurrency gave back all of its Nvidia rally in less than six hours, and now the Nasdaq has lost most of its upturn, the analysts say. The real test going forward is how long bitcoin struggles to hold around the $60,000 mark, they say. If it closes below the recent June low of $58,500, "this market would be in trouble and could trend down," the analysts say. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1137 ET - Crypto's rally alongside stocks on Monday proved short-lived as traders rush to take profits, FXPro's Alex Kuptsikevich says in a note. "Buyers remain unconvinced of a reversal," the analyst says. A more than 5% surge in bitcoin's price following Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia's CEO was completely erased within the following four hours, and on Tuesday morning, the price dropped below $59,400 twice, he says. Bitcoin is on its longest weekly losing streak since 2022, with traders now getting used to prices being below the 200-week moving average and the mining cost, which is around $75,000, Kuptsikevich says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1122 ET - Food inflation in advanced economies has been subdued despite this year's energy shock, in contrast to 2022 when the Russia-Ukraine war led to a 6 percentage-point increase after 10 months, Capital Economics's chief global economist Jennifer McKeown says in a note. Likely reasons include Russia and Ukraine being major global suppliers of agricultural commodities, whereas the Middle East is largely a food-importing region. Ample inventories of agricultural commodities entering the conflict with Iran helped cushion the impact of higher input costs, while stretched incomes led to intense price competition among supermarkets, keeping them from passing on higher costs. It's also early as the peak indirect impact on food of higher oil and gas prices comes after a lag of 12-18 months, according to the firm's estimates. "Food inflation will probably rise as higher energy costs feed through, but it should remain far below its 2022 peaks," McKeown adds. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1045 ET - Sterling could outperform the euro for longer if the U.K. economy continues to grow at a steady pace, MUFG's Lee Hardman says in a note. The U.K.'s better-than-expected growth and relatively high Bank of England interest rate at 4% have contributed to sterling's strength against the euro, Hardman says. "The combination of stronger U.K. growth and relatively high yields appears to be attracting more foreign capital, providing an additional source of support for the pound," he says. The euro rises 0.1% versus sterling to 0.8364 pounds, having hit a 19-month low of 0.8318 pounds last week, LSEG data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

1036 ET - French President Emmanuel Macron's proposal to help stabilize the country's fiscal outlook is unlikely to fix its problems, Charlotte de Montpellier at ING says in a note. The so-called "golden rule" would create multiyear framework laws, adding legal spending restraints to annual budgets. But the rule would fall short of setting a debt target, and a subsequent organic law would be needed to determine how compliance would be assessed. Furthermore, parliament could potentially make modifications, while approving the rule may not gain enough political support. "France's central problem...is less the absence of rules than the absence of political willingness to implement them." More important will be passing a credible budget, though this is easier said than done, de Montpellier says. (don.forbes@wsj.com)

1020 ET - Debt issued by AI-related companies dominates U.S. credit trading volume, Barclays' Zornitsa Todorova says in a note. AI bonds accounted for a record 22.3% of U.S. investment-grade customer volume in November, according to data through November 19, up from only 6% in 2024, Todorova says. AI issuers made up 8% of the U.S. high-yield trading volume in November, while accounting for 4% of the outstanding U.S. high-yield debt, she says. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0959 ET - The Turkish lira looks on course for further falls in 2027 as the central bank has resumed cutting interest rates despite elevated inflation, Commerzbank's Tatha Ghose says in a note. Policymakers can smooth the lira's depreciation path through foreign-exchange interventions at a significant cost but cannot change the trend, he says. Moreover, constant interventions consumes scarce forex reserves. Weak demand, high prices, expensive credit and exporters' loss of competitiveness are becoming part of the backdrop, putting pressure on the government ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections in 2028, he says. The dollar rises 0.6% to 50.6224 lira after earlier hitting a record high of 50.6354, according to LSEG. Commerzbank expects it to reach 64.80 lira by December 2027. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)
